issues.legal_issue: Circumstantial evidence must form a complete and conclusive chain before it can sustain a murder conviction.
material_facts: There was no eyewitness, and the prosecution case rested entirely on circumstantial evidence.
The evidence of an alleged illicit relationship did not establish who committed the killing.
No evidence showed the accused near the well immediately after the cries and sound of a fall; the deceased’s footwear was found beside the well.
The medical evidence did not establish that suffocation occurred before the fall, and the injuries could have resulted from the fall.
The alleged disclosures by the deceased to witnesses were hearsay, and the recovery of a saree and photograph did not establish guilt.
The evidence did not exclude the possibility of suicide, and the prosecution’s circumstances raised suspicion but left reasonable doubt.
issues.conclusion: The chain of circumstantial evidence was incomplete and incoherent, so the murder convictions could not safely be sustained; the accused were entitled to the benefit of doubt and the appeals were allowed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sharad Birdhichand Sarda v. State of Maharashtra (1984) 4 SCC 116, the circumstances must be conclusive, consistent only with guilt, and form a chain leaving no reasonable ground for a conclusion consistent with innocence. Sujit Biswas v. State of Assam (2013) 12 SCC 406 and Raja @ Rajendra v. State of Haryana (2015) 11 SCC 43 reaffirm that the circumstances, considered collectively, must lead only to the irresistible conclusion that the accused committed the crime; the chain’s completeness depends on the facts of each case. Suspicion, however grave, cannot substitute for proof.

predicates.criminal_appeal_from_conviction: The accused appealed a criminal conviction.
predicates.case_based_entirely_on_circumstantial_ev: The prosecution relied entirely on circumstances rather than eyewitness testimony.
predicates.circumstantial_chain_incomplete: The circumstances did not form a complete and conclusive chain pointing only to the accused’s guilt.
predicates.reasonable_innocent_explanation_remains: The evidence left a reasonable explanation consistent with the accused’s innocence.

issues.definition: When an accused appeals a conviction based entirely on circumstances, an incomplete chain or a remaining reasonable innocent explanation results in an unsustainable conviction and entitlement to the benefit of doubt.

issues.legal_issue: A spouse’s connection to the deceased does not, without evidence linking the spouse to the scene, justify an adverse inference from the spouse’s failure to explain a death occurring away from the home.
material_facts: The deceased’s body was found in a well away from his residence.
There was no evidence that either accused was seen near the well immediately after the cries and sound of a fall.
The prosecution sought to implicate the deceased’s wife, but the circumstances did not establish her presence at the scene at the relevant time.
issues.conclusion: No definitive presumption against the wife as a conspirator could be drawn on these facts by shifting the burden to her.
issues.legal_principle: Section 106 of the Evidence Act does not justify placing a burden on an accused spouse merely because the death concerns the spouse’s partner; in the circumstances here, the location of the death away from the residence and the absence of evidence placing the accused near the scene precluded a definitive presumption of guilt.

rule.if: criminal_case_relying_on_circumstantial_evidence and accused_is_deceaseds_spouse and death_scene_away_from_home and accused_not_shown_near_scene

predicates.criminal_case_relying_on_circumstantial_: The prosecution sought to prove criminal responsibility through circumstantial evidence.
predicates.accused_is_deceaseds_spouse: The accused was married to the person who died.
predicates.death_scene_away_from_home: The person’s death occurred at a location away from the shared or family residence.
predicates.accused_not_shown_near_scene: No evidence placed the accused near the scene at the relevant time.

issues.definition: When a circumstantial criminal case concerns a deceased person’s spouse, a death away from home and no evidence placing the spouse near the scene mean that failure to explain the death does not support an adverse inference.

issues.legal_issue: Oral testimony that written confessional statements were made does not supply incriminating proof when the alleged statements are not produced and proved.
material_facts: Two witnesses testified that the accused had made confessional statements at an official’s office and that the statements had been recorded in writing.
The prosecution did not produce or prove the alleged written statements.
One witness also acknowledged that he had not disclosed the alleged statements to anyone.
issues.conclusion: The witnesses’ oral testimony that the confessional statements had been recorded was of no consequence and substantially weakened the prosecution case.
issues.legal_principle: The Court treated the failure to produce and prove the alleged written confessional statements as substantially undermining their evidentiary value; oral testimony that the statements had been recorded was, by itself, of no consequence in the circumstances of this case.

predicates.criminal_case_using_alleged_confession: The prosecution relied on an alleged confession to support a criminal charge.
predicates.alleged_written_confession_not_produced_: The prosecution did not produce or prove the alleged written confession.
predicates.only_oral_testimony_confirms_recording: Witnesses testified that a confession had been recorded, but the alleged statement itself was not before the court as proved evidence.

issues.definition: In a criminal case relying on an alleged confession, when the written statement is not produced or proved and only oral testimony confirms its recording, that oral account has no incriminating value.
